KEY MESSAGE 1...

Current sfc analysis shows a strong pair of Canadian surface high 
pressure systems over the Great Lakes and south of James Bay, 
continuing to build into the region. Gradual decrease in moisture 
will allow for some partial clearing of clouds late this afternoon 
to evening, mainly in areas north of I-90, with coverage still 
persisting for areas south of Albany. After only reaching highs in 
the upper 50s (terrain) and upper 60s (valleys), about 5-10 degrees 
below normal this afternoon, temperatures will become cool after 
sunset. Even though low level moisture is decreasing, there will 
still be enough left along with a light breeze to limit radiational 
cooling compared to tomorrow night. Tonight, some patchy to 
localized areas of frost will occur over the southern ADKs and 
southern Greens with lows in the mid to upper 30s. The growing 
season ended yesterday for the southern ADKs, so no headlines there 
and after collaboration with neighboring offices, frost advisory 
criteria (33 to 36F) will not be met for our areas still within the 
growing season tonight with lows in the upper 30s to low 40s 
elsewhere. 

Fair and cool weather conditions continue tomorrow as a Rex Block 
begins to set up with a closed upper level high over south-central 
Ontario/northern Great Lakes region poleward of a closed low over 
the Ohio Valley and mid level trough over the Mid Atlantic states.
The sfc high will continue to dominate over the region with 
continued high temperatures below normal with mid to upper 60s in 
the valleys and mid 50s to lower 60s over the higher terrain. 
Conditions will be more ideal for a radiational cooling set-up with 
clear skies across most of the region, and calming winds tomorrow 
night. Lows in the mid 30s to about 40F is expected north of the 
Capital Region with some upper 30s also in the eastern/northern 
Catskills. Lower to mid 40s are expected from the Capital Region 
south and east and within most of the Mohawk Valley. Probabilistic 
guidance has about a 40 to 50% chance of min temps below 37F for 
areas where the growing season continues in the Southern ADKs, Lake 
George-Saratoga Region/Glens Falls area, and southern Vermont, 
suggesting patchy frost may become more widespread areas of frost 
tomorrow night which could meet frost advisory thresholds. Some 
patchy to localized areas of radiational fog will also be possible 
in the river valleys and sheltered locations. Pleasant fall weather 
continues on Thursday with the surface high overhead one more day as 
temperatures trend closer to seasonal. 

KEY MESSAGE 2... 

Attention shifts to a developing coastal cyclone Thu night/Fri 
morning near or east of the Carolinas. Multiple shortwave patterns 
later this week will try to aid in the enhancement of the low 
pressure system as it meanders along the East Coast undergoing 
cyclogensis, eventually closing off Friday-Friday night east of the 
Mid Atlantic states and south of Long Island/southern New England. 
The track, evolution and timing of rain, winds and coastal impacts 
vary still on the ensembles, deterministic medium range guidance and 
the EC/GFS AI and depending on how close the low tracks toward 
Eastern New York and Western New England. One solution shows track 
well offshore impacting southeast New England and Cape Cod at best. 
The European ensemble and AI show a third track of the low shifting 
further west towards New Jersey. A third cluster, and the most 
favored track at this time has the low tracking  closer to southeast 
New England and Long Island for intermittent bands of showers 
(mainly light to moderate) and breezy conditions Fri afternoon 
through Saturday especially from the Capital Region/Hudson River 
Valley south and east. Overall, confidence is low with the track, 
but there is medium confidence that winds will become gusty from the 
north/northeast Friday-Saturday. 

Our forecast currently favors the NBM into Fri and the WPC Day 4-7 
guidance incorporated thereafter. The north/northeast winds begin to 
increase Friday night through Saturday. Probabilistic NBM guidance 
in the Friday-Saturday timeframe has a 30 to 40% chance for 30-35 
mph gusts for southern areas in the Mid Hudson Valley and a 40 to 
50% chance for 30-35 mph gusts in southwest New England, especially 
in areas of higher terrain (Taconics, Litchfield Hills, and 
Catskills). These winds could blow around unsecured outdoors objects 
or knock down some foliated smaller tree limbs. The chances of 
impactful rainfall are low with probabilities of rainfall south and 
east of the Capital Region showing about a 30% chance for 1" or 
greater through 8am Monday. Slight deviations will make a difference 
over the next few days so trends will continue to be monitored. 
Temps will be near normal through the weekend.
